title: Conventions in the Book
output-file: book-conventions.html
# Quarto would infer this from the single `{r}` cell below, but pinning it
# keeps the page from silently reverting to the jupyter engine if that cell is
# ever removed — which would also change where a Python warning is reported.
# knitr runs the `{python}` cells through reticulate, which finds the uv venv
# from VIRTUAL_ENV as long as the book is rendered under `uv run`.
engine: knitr
---

```{r}
#| include: false
# Optional — the page renders without this chunk.
#
# knitr pulls reticulate in by itself the first time it meets a `{python}`
# cell, and reticulate finds the uv venv from VIRTUAL_ENV whenever the book is
# rendered with `uv run`, which is what the Makefile does. This chunk is here
# to make that dependency visible in the source rather than implicit, and to
# still resolve the right interpreter if someone renders outside `uv run`,
# where VIRTUAL_ENV is not set. `required = FALSE` means a missing .venv is
# ignored rather than an error, so the chunk can never be what breaks a render.
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv(here::here(".venv"), required = FALSE)
```

One page holding every construct the book uses, so a theme or CSS change can be
checked in one place, in both light and dark mode.
This is a good reference page for how source code renders to the page.

You can learn more about features in the [Quarto Guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/).

## Text

Body text, with **bold**, *italic*, `inline code`,
a [link to another page](1-MDStools-bash-filesystem.qmd)
and an [external link](https://quarto.org).
Keyboard keys are written with `<kbd>`.
Named keys take title case: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>, <kbd>Shift</kbd>, <kbd>Tab</kbd>,
<kbd>Enter</kbd>, <kbd>Esc</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd>, <kbd>Up</kbd>,
<kbd>Down</kbd>.
A letter key stays lowercase unless <kbd>Shift</kbd> is genuinely part of the
shortcut, so that an uppercase letter never implies a <kbd>Shift</kbd> that
isn't there: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>c</kbd> interrupts a command, while
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>C</kbd> opens the browser console.
The same rule reads correctly for a program that treats case as meaning,
such as <kbd>n</kbd> and <kbd>N</kbd> in `less`.
Enough of them to wrap, so their boxes can be checked against each other on
neighbouring lines:
press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>c</kbd> to stop a running command,
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>d</kbd> to close the shell,
<kbd>Tab</kbd> to complete a path,
<kbd>Up</kbd> and <kbd>Down</kbd> to walk back through your history,
and <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>r</kbd> to search it.

## Code

Every static listing carries a label saying where its contents belong, and the
copy button says whether you are meant to take it: a listing you run or paste
has one, a listing showing what the machine said back does not.

| You are looking at | Fence | Label | Copy button |
|---|---|---|---|
| a command to run in the terminal | `bash` | automatic | yes |
| what the terminal printed back | `out` | automatic | no |
| code in a file, or typed at a console | `python`, `r` | `filename` | yes |
| the contents of a file | its own language, or `default` | `filename` | yes |

`bash` and `out` are labelled by `code-labels.lua`, because those two labels
never vary. Everything else says where it belongs with an explicit `filename`,
because that is where a label earns its keep -- `penguins.py` and
`pyproject.toml` tell you something "Python" and "TOML" do not.

A command and what it printed, which is the pairing most of the book is made
of. They are two listings, never one, so the command can be copied without
dragging the output along with it:

```bash
ls
```

```out
Applications    Pictures
Desktop         Documents       Movies
Downloads       Music
```

A listing that is a file, labelled with the file's name:

```{.python filename="penguins.py"}
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

penguins = load_penguins()
print(penguins.head())
```

```{.toml filename="pyproject.toml"}
[project]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
```

A file with no language of its own. `default` is the fence for these: no
highlighting, but still a copy button, because it is a listing you are meant to
put somewhere:

```{.default filename=".python-version"}
3.14
```

A listing typed at a console rather than saved to a file:

```{.r filename="R Console"}
install.packages(c("xaringan", "revealjs"))
```

The remaining languages, which reach the page the same way:

```yaml
# yaml listing, used for _quarto.yml and the GitHub Actions workflow
project:
  type: website
```

```markdown
# markdown listing
```

```{.json filename="sample_notebook.ipynb"}
{"cells": [{"cell_type": "markdown", "source": ["# A heading"]}]}
```

```
# a bare fence: no label, no highlighting, no copy button
```

A listing wider than the page, so the horizontal scrollbar can be checked.
Real lines in the book reach about 150 characters:

```bash
uv run --with 'numpy>=2.5.2' --with 'matplotlib>=3.11.1' python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" --directory ~/a/deeply/nested/project/path
```

Output wide enough to scroll, so the same can be checked on the quieter
surface:

```out
cpython-3.14.7-macos-aarch64-none    /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14 -> ../Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.7/bin/python3.14
```

A one-line command and a one-line output, the shortest the pairing gets:

```bash
uv --version
```

```out
uv 0.12.6
```

### Executed cells

A cell and its output:

```{python}
# python code
a = 3
a**2
```

A cell showing its own fence, which is how the book explains chunk options:

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
a + 1
```

An R cell and its output. The page is pinned to the knitr engine in the front
matter, so the Python cells above run through reticulate, which picks up the
uv venv from `VIRTUAL_ENV` when the book is rendered with `uv run`:

```{r}
# r code
a <- 1:5
a^2
```

A cell that writes to stderr, which Quarto puts in an output block of its own.
This one is R, because under knitr a Python warning arrives on stdout instead:

```{r}
warning("a warning from a cell")
```

A cell whose output is a figure:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
```

:::

:::

:::

:::

:::{.exercise}

:::

:::{.activity}
An activity!
:::

:::{.exercise}
Another exercise!
:::

:::{.activity}
Another activity!
:::

Callouts hold listings too, and Quarto styles those differently from a listing
out in the body:

:::{.callout-note}
A note with a listing in it:

```bash
ls -la
```
:::
